newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China opens to Hong Kong Democrats for first time.
newsitem.headline: China opens to Hong Kong Democrats for first time.

text.p: China opened its doors to its arch-foes in Hong Kong on Friday, allowing the Democratic Party to enter Beijing's mission to hand over a petition urging China to oust Japan from the disputed Diaoyu islands.
It was the first time that members of the party, which often stages rowdy protests against Beijing outside the building, had crossed the metal barricades and entered the foyer.
The event comes soon after Beijing sent out signals it was willing to start a dialogue with the party, which would represent a major turnabout after years of hostility.

The Democrats have been a thorn in China's side because of their unrelenting campaign for full democracy in Hong Kong after China takes the colony back from Britain next year, and because of their support for dissidents in China.

"If we were asking China to develop democracy in Hong Kong or to improve its human rights record, then I think the reception would have been quite different," said Yeung Sum, deputy chairman of the Democratic Party.
"But in this case, we're asking the Chinese government to take tougher action in protecting its sovereignty over Chinese territory," he said.

Brandishing banners with slogans such as "Japan must leave the Diaoyu Islands" and "China must protect her territory", a group of about 30 demonstrators waved clenched fists and chanted nationalistic slogans.
"Diaoyu belongs to China," they shouted in unison as a contingent of police looked on.

In a letter to Qiao Shi, chairman of the National People's Congress, or parliament, the Democratic Party urged China to take diplomatic action against "Japan's invasion of Chinese territory." It also demanded the Tokyo government apologize.
"The Chinese government has been too soft in dealing with the Japanese occupation of the Diaoyu Islands because it wants Japan to be involved in China's economic development," Yeung said.

Earlier, up to 40 members and backers of Hong Kong's pro-China party, the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong, rallied for the first time outside the Chinese mission. It was an unprecedented outpouring of frustration over perceived inertia by China.
